stimulus: Ecologist: Streams in the Harlow watershed show mayfly counts forty percent below their ten-year average. Farm runoff is the usual suspect in such declines, and this watershed does border cropland. Yet the better explanation is last summer's channel-dredging project: mayfly larvae anchor in gravel beds, and the dredging stripped those beds from long stretches of the streams. It was the dredging, not runoff, that depressed the mayfly population.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ecologist's argument?
choice_a: Mayfly counts in the Harlow watershed began falling within weeks of the start of the dredging project.
choice_b: Streams in a neighboring watershed that were never dredged showed a similar decline in mayfly counts over the same period.
choice_c: Insect populations of many kinds have declined across the region over the past decade.
choice_d: Water sampled monthly throughout the decline showed agricultural chemical concentrations no higher than in years when mayfly counts were normal.
choice_e: Mayflies are an important food source for several fish species native to the Harlow watershed.
prediction_text: Look for evidence that eliminates the named rival - farm runoff - rather than merely restating support for dredging.
trap_a: timing correlation compatible with either cause (survivor)
explanation_a: Timing consistent with dredging is also consistent with a season of runoff; it does not separate the two causes.
explanation_b: A matching decline where no dredging occurred points away from dredging as the explanation; this weakens.
explanation_c: A regionwide, decade-long trend concerns a different scope and cannot arbitrate between these two local causes.
explanation_d: Correct. Normal chemical levels during the decline remove runoff from contention, leaving the dredging explanation stronger.
explanation_e: The ecological role of mayflies is irrelevant to which cause reduced their numbers.
